name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,139

clue.text: Congratulatory gesture seconds before friend returned

indicators.note: something returned has come back the way it went, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: someone who has returned is back, so the word also supplies these letters
S is the standard abbreviation for seconds
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: Someone races to a returning friend to give a hearty congratulatory gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' does double duty: as 'back' it supplies the opening letters, and it also turns the friend round.
explanation.definitionFit: Clapping someone on the shoulders is a familiar physical show of praise after a success.

clue.text: Infant left on “wonderful” location

blocks.note: an infant is a baby
L is the usual abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: A baby has been left in some marvellous spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'wonderful' flag a pun: the Hanging Gardens of this ancient city were one of the Seven Wonders of the World.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Mesopotamian city housed the Hanging Gardens, counted among the Seven Wonders of antiquity.

clue.text: Ocean tossed around small vessel

indicators.note: things tossed around land jumbled, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Heavy seas throw a little boat about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like it might signal a container, but it belongs with 'tossed' as one rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A light narrow boat paddled by hand is a typical example of a little craft.

clue.text: Appear to be fully employed in the field of entertainment

blocks.note: to appear is to show up
read as busy-ness, the state of being fully occupied

explanation.surface: Someone wants to look busy while working in entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is read as 'busy-ness', so the wordplay means 'show that you are busy', which is what appearing fully employed amounts to.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre, film and television together make up the industry of performers and promoters.

clue.text: Passage in church I will broadcast

indicators.note: a broadcast is something heard rather than seen, so we go by sound

blocks.note: the contraction of these words, spoken

explanation.surface: Someone vows to announce something in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I will' contracts to I'LL, which is pronounced the same as the church passage.
explanation.definitionFit: The walkway between rows of pews, down which a bride walks, is the classic church passage.

clue.text: Unaccompanied male’s second name

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a tag is a label or name

explanation.surface: A man on his own gives his middle name.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay. Going 'stag' means attending a party without a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A man who attends a social event without a female partner is said to go stag.

clue.text: Attendant upset four in city in Israel

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so letters read from the bottom up

blocks.note: a valet is a personal attendant
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A hotel attendant upsets four guests in an Israeli city.
explanation.walkthrough: VALET runs backwards to TELAV, then the Roman numeral for four completes the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Israel's second-largest city sits on the Mediterranean coast and is its commercial hub.

clue.text: Grow old, say, after turning 100

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: e.g. means 'for example', which is what 'say' means
a ton is slang for a hundred

explanation.surface: Someone muses about ageing after reaching their hundredth birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning 100' reads like reaching a centenary, but 'turning' reverses the example abbreviation, and 100 is a ton.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb is an idiom for advancing in years, as in 'she is getting on a bit'.

clue.text: Denmark great for development as place to sell fruit and veg

definitions.text: place to sell fruit and veg
definitions.note: loose: a market garden grows produce for sale

indicators.note: something under development is being reshaped, so the letters are rebuilt into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Denmark is ripe for development as a hub for selling produce.
explanation.walkthrough: The country name and 'great' together supply all twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a smallholding where vegetables and fruit are grown commercially, to be sold at markets.

clue.text: Discard attempt in game

blocks.note: to bin something is to throw it away
a go is a try

explanation.surface: A player throws away a turn during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discard' sounds like a card-game move, but it is the verb meaning to throw away.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a numbers game of chance where players mark off called numbers on a card.

clue.text: Red mark on skin from really minor injury?

blocks.note: a scar is a mark left on the skin
-let is a diminutive suffix, as in piglet, so this is a tiny version of the mark

explanation.surface: A red mark on the skin is put down to a trivial injury.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the whimsy: a very small scar would be a 'scar-let', using the suffix that makes things little.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a bright vivid shade of the colour, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Shelter from swimmer going the wrong way

indicators.note: travelling in the wrong direction means heading backwards, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: an eel is a swimming fish

explanation.surface: Someone takes refuge from a swimmer heading the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' suggests a person, but it is a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The lee is the sheltered side away from the wind, as in the lee of a hill.

clue.text: Avoid losing money from holiday flat

blocks.note: a break is a short holiday
flat and even both mean level

explanation.surface: Someone hopes to stay out of the red by letting out a holiday apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment noun, but it is the adjective meaning level.
explanation.definitionFit: To end with income equal to costs is to make neither profit nor loss.

clue.text: Most pleasant flying insect

indicators.note: flying things scatter in the air, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone praises a flying bug as the loveliest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying insect' reads as one phrase naming a creature; 'flying' is really the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of an everyday adjective for agreeable or delightful.

clue.text: Connected up Echo, Tango, Charlie

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: Echo is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for E
taken as written
Charlie is the phonetic alphabet word for C

explanation.surface: A radio operator has connected up a string of call signs.
explanation.walkthrough: The phonetic alphabet supplies single letters, but Tango is kept whole; the string is then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes things related by common origin, such as languages or words sharing a root.

clue.text: Makes great effort to lose Romeo in Cornish town

indicators.note: losing something means it goes missing, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: to strive is to try hard
Romeo is the phonetic alphabet word for R

explanation.surface: Someone works hard to shake off a lover while in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo suggests the lover, but it is the call sign for R. Cornwall is the county at England's south-western tip.
explanation.definitionFit: This seaside resort in Cornwall is known for its artists' colony and beaches.

clue.text: Grimaced, as small farmyard animal was ahead

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a cow is a farm animal
to be ahead in a race is to have led

explanation.surface: Someone pulled a face because a little farm animal had got in front.
explanation.walkthrough: The three pieces simply join in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe twisting the face into an expression of displeasure or anger.

clue.text: Muscular gent inappropriately entertains country

indicators.note: to entertain is to host guests inside, so the words hold the letters within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A beefy man behaves improperly in hosting a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inappropriately' looks like a scramble signal, but it is just part of the string that contains the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American nation, capital Buenos Aires, is simply an example of a country.

clue.text: Fury in most of French city

indicators.note: taking most but not all means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: A city in the Loire valley of France

explanation.surface: Rage erupts across much of a French city.
explanation.walkthrough: The city is written like the English plural, but it is a French place name; dropping its last letter leaves the emotion.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns name a strong feeling of rage and hostility, so they are direct synonyms.

clue.text: One’s to make legal claim for children

blocks.note: one is I, and the apostrophe-s adds S
to sue is to bring a legal claim

explanation.surface: A parent intends to go to court over custody of the children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' links the wordplay to the definition, which sits at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: In legal and formal language, a person's offspring or descendants are called their issue.

clue.text: Very eager to finish early in the past

indicators.note: finishing early means stopping before the end, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: agog means eagerly excited

explanation.surface: Someone who was keen to wrap up early, back in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for very eager loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means before now, as in 'years ago', placing something earlier in time.

clue.text: Gold pens stop working in farewell

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a machine that dies stops working

explanation.surface: Golden fountain pens fail during a goodbye letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' reads as writing instruments but is the verb meaning encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the French word for goodbye, used in English as a formal parting.

clue.text: Good girls in spectacles

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
lasses are girls, especially in Scotland and northern England

explanation.surface: Well-behaved young women wearing eyewear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but it only joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeglasses and spectacles are interchangeable everyday words for lenses worn to correct vision.

clue.text: Sick following doctor’s training exercise

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so the piece named first in the clue is placed second

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
sick means ill

explanation.surface: A patient feels unwell after the doctor's fitness routine.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A drill is a routine practised repeatedly, as in a fire drill or military parade practice.

clue.text: Grass on editor

blocks.note: re means on or concerning, as in business letters
ed is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: Someone informs on a newspaper editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' suggests the British slang for informing, but it is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Reeds are tall water-growing plants belonging to the grass family.

clue.text: Bruce and Dicky’s vegetarian paste

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for unsound or faulty, so the letters are in a broken order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two men named Bruce and Dicky share a meatless spread.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a second name beside Bruce, but it is the British word for unreliable or shaky; the apostrophe-s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tofu is a soft curd pressed from soya milk and a staple protein for those avoiding meat.
